title: Pressure & Soft Washing | North Central Florida
description: Pressure washing and soft washing in North Central Florida for siding, stucco, roofs, drives, and decks. Kills mildew and algae without damaging paint.
h1: Pressure Washing and Soft Washing in North Central Florida
heroIntro: The right cleaning method for each surface: low-pressure soft washing for painted walls and roofs, higher pressure for concrete. It kills mildew and algae and leaves the coating intact.
card: Soft washing for siding and roofs, pressure washing for concrete. Clean surfaces, no damage to paint.

questions: What is the difference between soft washing and pressure washing?

sections.h2: Soft washing vs. pressure washing: picking the method
body: The green film on a north wall and the black streaks under a gutter are living growth: algae, mildew, and mold. High pressure blasts the top layer off but leaves the roots, and the stain is back in a few months. On painted siding and stucco it also forces water behind the coating, lifts caulk, and can etch soft stucco. The damage only shows once things dry.

Soft washing uses low pressure and a cleaning solution that kills the growth, then gives it time to work before a gentle rinse. It is the method for painted siding, stucco, roofs, screen enclosures, and anything with a coating you want to keep. Pressure washing with surface cleaners and higher pressure is reserved for hard surfaces like concrete drives, sidewalks, pool decks, and pavers. Both fall under the same service, and the estimate states which method goes on which surface.
Most of our washing work falls into a few groups. Each one gets the method and dwell time that suits it.

body: Every exterior paint job we do starts with a wash. Paint will not hold to chalky, dirty, or mildewed walls, and any growth left under a new coat will come back through it. When the wash is part of an exterior painting project, we schedule enough dry time after cleaning that the surface is ready for primer. Stucco and wood can hold water for a day or more after a thorough wash, and we check before coating.

Decks and fences need a slightly different approach. A wood cleaner and brightener removes graying and old stain residue so new stain soaks in evenly; the details are on our deck and fence staining page.

sections.h2: Florida-specific problems: pollen, rust, and mildew
body: Spring brings a yellow-green coat of oak and pine pollen that sticks to screens, windows, and cars and leaves stains on light surfaces. Our article on cleaning Florida pollen stains covers what works. Irrigation from well water leaves orange rust streaks on stucco and concrete that need a specific treatment rather than more pressure. And shaded, damp walls grow mildew year-round; if you are not sure whether what you see is dirt or growth, read our guide to mold on siding.

We control rinse water so runoff is diluted and kept away from plantings, and we cover or pre-wet sensitive landscaping before applying cleaning solution. Eco-conscious cleaning options are available if you have a vegetable garden, a koi pond, or pets that spend time in the yard.

sections.h2: What a wash visit looks like
body: Before any cleaning starts, we walk the property and note what needs protecting: outdoor outlets and light fixtures, open windows and vents, delicate plants, pool equipment, and painted surfaces that are already peeling. Windows and doors are checked closed, and electrical covers are sealed where needed.

The cleaning solution is applied from the bottom up so it does not streak, given time to work on the growth, then rinsed from the top down. Concrete is cleaned with a rotary surface cleaner so you do not end up with the wand stripes that come from a handheld nozzle. Rust and stubborn stains get a targeted treatment afterward. We finish with a walk around the house to check for missed spots, and we rinse plantings again before we leave.

If the wash turns up failing paint, soft wood, or cracked stucco, we point it out and photograph it. Washing often reveals problems that were hidden under the dirt, and it is better to know about them before the next storm season.

sections.h2: How often to wash and how to book it
body: In North Central Florida, most houses benefit from a soft wash every year or two, sooner on shaded lots or walls near sprinklers. Regular washing also extends the life of your paint, because algae holds moisture against the coating. Most homes are washed in a single day, and you do not need to be home as long as we can reach an outdoor water spigot and the gates are unlocked.
Washing can be booked on its own or added to a paint or stain project. Local information is on our Gainesville pressure washing and Ocala pressure washing pages.

faqs.q: What is the difference between soft washing and pressure washing?
faqs.a: Soft washing uses low pressure and a cleaning solution that kills mildew and algae, and is used on painted siding, stucco, and roofs. Pressure washing uses higher pressure and is reserved for hard surfaces like concrete and pavers.

faqs.q: Can pressure washing damage my paint or stucco?
faqs.a: High pressure can force water behind paint, lift caulk, and etch soft stucco. That is why painted walls and stucco get a soft wash instead.

faqs.q: How often should a house be washed in Florida?
faqs.a: Every one to two years for most homes, more often on shaded lots or walls hit by sprinklers. Regular washing also helps paint last longer.
Yes. Every exterior paint project starts with a wash and mildew treatment, followed by enough dry time before primer goes on.
